name: Treaty with the Omaha, 1854
promises: The Omaha kept the country north of the cession line as their future home; if the President moved them, a new home of no more than 300,000 acres (Article 1).

Annuities of $40,000 a year for three years, $30,000 a year for ten years, $20,000 a year for fifteen years and $10,000 a year for twelve years, the President deciding how much went in money and how much to education, farming and supplies (Article 4).
$41,000 more to settle, move and subsist for a year, including fencing and breaking 200 acres (Article 5).
The United States to protect the Omaha from the Sioux and all other hostile tribes for as long as the President judged necessary (Article 7).
A grist and sawmill with a miller, a blacksmith shop with a smith, and a farmer for ten years (Article 8).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found the 4,982,097.87 acres ceded by this treaty were worth 75 cents an acre, $3,736,573.40, on April 17, 1854, held that the $975,739.54 paid for them was unconscionable, and awarded the difference, $2,760,833.86. After a $25,000 offset the final award was $2,735,833.86 (May 6, 1959).

landTaken: 4,982,097.87 acres in northeastern Nebraska, including all of Cedar, Pierce, Wayne, Stanton, Cuming, Dakota, Dodge, Washington, Douglas, Burt and Sarpy counties and parts of others (Docket 225-A, finding 31).
compensation: The Commission found $975,739.54 was paid. It disallowed a claimed offset of $374,465.02, allowed a stipulated offset of $25,000, and entered a final award of $2,735,833.86 on May 6, 1959.
today: The claimant was the Omaha Tribe of Nebraska. Later reductions of the reservation kept by this treaty are separate queue entries (kappler-880, 1865; cession-1874-06-22-omaha; cession-1882-08-07-omaha).

nationVoice.summary: In a 2013 release on the Pender boundary case, the Tribe said its reservation was established in 1854 by treaty with the United States with original boundaries covering all of present-day Thurston County, that an 1865 treaty ceded the northern part for the Winnebago, and that it was defending the undiminished reservation in court against claims that an 1882 law had shrunk it.

plain.promised: The country north of the cession line as the Omaha's home, yearly payments, money to move and settle, a mill, blacksmith and farmer, and protection from the Sioux and other hostile tribes.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1958 that the 4,982,097.87 acres ceded were worth $3,736,573.40, and that the $975,739.54 paid for them was unconscionable.
plain.today: The Commission entered a final award of $2,735,833.86 on May 6, 1959. Whether it was paid has not been traced. Later reductions of the Omaha reservation are recorded separately.

openQuestions: The Commission's finding 30 cites the treaty as 10 Stat. 1093 in the OCR text; Kappler and the OSU edition give 10 Stat. 1043.
Whether the Article 7 promise of protection from the Sioux was kept was not researched; Omaha Docket 225-C (1957 opinion, pointer 17) may bear on it.
The Omaha Tribe of Nebraska's website (omaha-nsn.gov) did not respond in this pass, so the Nation's own account is not linked yet.
The queue lists Royce Areas 315, 637, 467, 570 and 636 for this id; the award covers the 1854 cession only. Which Royce number the Commission's 4,982,097.87 acres match was not confirmed.

Audit 2026-11-08: treaty articles 1, 4, 5, 7 and 8 and every Docket 225-A figure checked and held. The note that the Nation's own account is not linked is out of date: nationVoice carries the Tribe's 2013 release.
